author: Miles_Brundage
text: Standardization of solar plant design/construction processes has myriad benefits soft cost-wise but conflicts w/ other plant improvements.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: PV plants are similar to each other in many ways, + some tasks are similar to each other, but the differences are sufficient to require ML.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The reason for the "==>", briefly, is that w/o ML, you spend a ton of time/$ on automating X, then next plant is different. Not scalable.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: One of the key probs with solar construction automation is the diversity of tasks across and within plants ==> machine learning will be key.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Human pro Go play (/future superhuman Go AI) "not as simple as a trade-off between exploitation-exploration or ... compressibility." - Ibid.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Pro Go players take more of the global context into account and make unexpected local decisions as a result. Various implications. - Ibid.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Go players going from amateur to professional become more predictable bc making fewer dumb local errors bc RL, then pros mix it up. - Ibid.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: "[C]hanging emphasis on local versus global context is expressed in how dependent the next move is on the stones ... played locally." Ibid.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: One of the coolest papers on Go I've read - "The Aggregate Complexity of Decisions in the Game of Go," Harre et al: http://t.co/8QXxkCPQxl

author: Miles_Brundage
text: There's a ridiculous amount of knowledge of Go heuristics, strategies, endgames, ko stuff, etc but non-trivial to integrate it in real-time.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Go is a very interesting/difficult game. First time I played it, I was overwhelmed by the branching factor/tradeoffs...full board soon! :)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Even for expert human Go players, there is no straightforward way to compare a few very good options with pros/cons over hundreds of moves.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Another big problem with computer Go is the lack of good evaluation functions/heuristics etc. and tradeoff btwn detail + simulation quantity

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Human feedback is already part of top Go systems in some sense, e.g. learning from human experts' games, maybe needs to be more substantial.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: In Go, a move's full consequences may not be understood for hundreds of moves. Makes MCTS helpful but insufficient bc always miss something.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: As Gelly et al. 2012 argue, MCTS combines good aspects of minimax and Monte Carlo, but probabilistic methods also have/make vulnerabilities.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Hand-coded rules/heuristics are nice in Go but hard to resolve conflicts/prioritize them. MCTS/NNs help but occasionally make huge mistakes.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Hand-coded heuristics, domain knowledge, etc. were once successful in Go. Simulation-based methods are now better but may need synthesis.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The Maddison et al. 2014 neural networks for Go move evaluation paper, for example, makes clear that more NN depth makes a HUGE difference.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: For people without much hardware to play with (i.e. most people not at big tech cos), MCTS/NNs hard to use to anywhere near their potential.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Neural nets seem likely to supplant or at least supplement other pattern recognition methods in computer Go but require tons of C/GPU power.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: In light of the compute power-intensiveness of MCTS and neural nets, to the extent those are key for Go, Google et al. have big advantages.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: As with AI in general, though, "integration" is easier said than done... Hence "plausible" :-)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: One plausible scenario for rapid Go progress: integration of the best of human Go knowledge/heuristics/GOFAI with the best of NNs/MCTS/etc.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Putting my last few tweets differently: simulation, self-play, MCTS, NNs, etc. great for Go but something else needed to get to superhuman.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Novel (crowdsourced? expert?) human-in-the-loop methods for critiquing Go systems' proposed move evaluations could also accelerate progress.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: MCTS now well established as useful in Go (and elsewhere); NNs now super helpful for move evaluation; GOFAI/heuristics needed 4 full system.

text: All of last few tweets, FWIW, are specific to 2015-2016. *Eventually,* AIs may be able to learn rules of most complex games on own, not yet.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: In general, more complex games/bigger state spaces/harder AI probs/etc. are easier to mess up, =need human feedback at various time-scales.

text: If DeepMind really wants to move to more and more complex games, they will need a good system for human input. Signs they're working on it.

text: Changes in learning shots matter more in real world vs. in simulation. Robot that learns 1st time vs. n-th time in real vs. simulated world.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Marginal changes in learning shots matter more when shots are fewer. Compare 1 vs 2 times teaching robot to do X, to 100 vs 101 data points.

text: Deep learning requires lots of "shots" of learning, but not (inherently) much human effort. Trainability, with e.g. Baxter, different. (2/2)

text: The human-effort-to-produce-result metric for AI progress is important but also importantly diff. from # of shots in machine learning. (1/2)

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The amount of human effort required to produce an AI ability from scratch or train an AI to do X is big metric, especially for $$$ purposes.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Whether AI ability/task/etc. X is amenable to progress-through-speed is one factor. Another such factor: human effort required to produce X.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Sidenote: will have working paper on AI progress soon, and slides after AAAI, but for now still thinking/tweeting through some key issues :)

text: Lack full view of AI prog/speed still but have some ideas: planning solvers/NNs/CSP more speed-friendly than architecture, commonsense, etc.

text: So the speed/AI progress connection is complex, but generally I think it's extremely fruitful and I plan to use it to clarify lots of stuff.

text: Last tweet is from the optimistic and reasonable conclusion to the Maddison et al. paper. Basically says what I said: Impressive, w caveats.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: "2 core elements that scale effectively w increased [compute]: scalable planning, using [MC]; and scalable eval functions, using deep NNs."

author: Miles_Brundage
text: "remarkable that a single, unified, straightforward architecture can master [a bunch of Go stuff] to such a degree [caveats..]" the Google 1

author: Miles_Brundage
text: One takeaway from the deep neural net/Go stuff for me is that while neural nets can't do everything, they can do a lot, more + more easily.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Maybe If I knew more re: neural nets, Go, and supercomps I could say for sure, but for now I dunno how long human Go supremacy will last. :/

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Even with, say, 20 or 100 layer neural networks, it isn't obvious how far heuristics/neural nets can take you in Go (/in general ;) )...

author: Miles_Brundage
text: To the extent that Maddison et al. were just using a tiny fraction of Google's resources for that paper, scaling up a lot/soon = more likely

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Clark and Storkey say they ran their system for a day at one point, Maddison et al. say they used GPUs/which algos but not how many/how long

author: Miles_Brundage
text: That being said, people keep coming up with ways to apply neural nets to new stuff, so maybe a more deeply neural netty system is possible.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: ..but it's far from perfect and will never be perfect, cuz the search space is huge. So other methods are needed to do other move analysis.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: The role of neural nets in the broader Go systems these folks are making is basically to provide a high quality heuristic for move quality..

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Also note that the papers I mentioned on Go do discuss other cool stuff/methods, Maddison uses Monte Carlo etc. But focusing here on NNs.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Also, on that sub-linear thing - not clear how important that metric was anyway, just one of the one ways they explicitly evaluate by depth.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Reasonable to infer based on Clark and Storkey and Maddison et al. (both 2014) that more computers would help a lot, dunno exactly how much.

author: Miles_Brundage
text: + success, but other metrics matter too, and it's unclear (to me at least) the relationship btwn those and overall skill. But >CPU/GPU helps

author: Miles_Brundage
text: From looking at the data in Maddison et al. 2014 (the DeepMind Go one), there is a sub-linear relationship btwn net depth and one metric of+

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Important to know how far deep neural nets can be scaled both up (supercomputers of present/future) and down (desktop, mobile, IoT, etc.).

author: Miles_Brundage
text: Would be good to have detailed understanding of, given some efficiency assumptions, what's plausible for diff NN depths in different domains

text: So, we know that you can get super impressive human-ish results out of 12 layer neural network, + human adjustment etc. What about 5? 20?
